overview.text: The Monocled Cobra is a dangerously venomous cobra of South and South-east Asia. It is named after the single ring - like a monocle, a one-eyed pair of glasses - on the back of its hood. It often lives near people and causes many snakebites in its range.

identification.text: Usually an O-shaped ring on the back of the hood (the Indian Cobra has a 'spectacles' mark instead), though the mark can vary or be missing. The body may be yellow, brown, grey or blackish, with or without cross-bands.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: From north-eastern India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh east through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam to southern China and the north of the Malay Peninsula.

habitat.text: Prefers places near water - rice paddies, swamps and mangroves - but also grassland, scrub, forest, farmland and even cities, up to about 1,000 m.

behaviour.text: Lives on the ground and is most active at dusk. In rice fields it hides in rat burrows in the banks. When disturbed it would rather escape; if cornered it rears up, spreads its hood, hisses loudly and strikes.

diet.text: Young cobras eat mostly frogs and toads; adults eat small mammals, other snakes and fish.

reproduction.text: Lays 16 to 33 eggs, usually between January and March. The eggs hatch after about 55 to 73 days, and the female usually stays with them.

recognise.text: A single ring ('monocle') on the back of the hood.
Spreads a wide hood when threatened.
